summary:
Casanare department stands under the national framework of Colombia, and the sources record no departmental legal regime of its own. The formal legal position a trans visitor meets in Casanare is therefore the national one: since the rule change approved in June 2015 the sex marker on government-issued identification has been changed by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments, and Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement.

National identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025, and passports issued within Colombia have offered three gender options, male, female and X, since August 2023. Adults may change legal gender before a notary without surgery, with a free simultaneous name change on the first request.

The formal protections are substantial. Homosexuality was decriminalised nationally in 1981, Congress passed a law banning discrimination based on sexual orientation in 2011, and the Constitutional Court legalised same-sex marriage in a 6-3 ruling of 28 April 2016, the first wedding taking place in Cali on 24 May 2016. Same-sex couples have held full adoption rights since a November 2015 ruling, and judgments T-314 of 2011, T-909 of 2011 and T-301 of 2004 protect entry to public and commercial premises against exclusion on grounds of gender identity.

The gap between formal protection and daily experience is lethal and is documented nationally. Thirteen trans people were killed in the first quarter of 2025, the Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025, more than 40 transgender women were killed in 2023, and eight trans women were killed between February and April 2024. On 5 April 2025 Sara Millerey, 32, drowned in a creek outside Medellín in Bello, Antioquia after being thrown in unable to swim with fractured legs, arms and hands; her mother Sandra Borja said "They killed her for being who she was," and President Petro ordered an urgent investigation. Reporting of 6 August 2025 documents that the killings did not stop after that case, with gangs linked to queer and transgender deaths.

A visitor to Casanare should expect these national patterns to apply: the department records no separate finding, and Casanare falls under the national kill figures and the armed-group pattern documented elsewhere in Colombia.
tangentialFactors:
Some of the targeting is organised by armed groups operating across departments. In Caquetá department, a different department with no Casanare-specific finding of its own, flyers on the streets and via WhatsApp named "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets in a "social cleansing" campaign reported on 30 July 2024. A trans woman and local election candidate was told by three armed men she had one week to leave town, hid for a week, then fled at night; a second trans woman said a friend had been killed.

In Guajira, armed groups have posted flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals since March 2024, stating that "all will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". These campaigns are cited here as evidence of the wider pattern a visitor to Casanare would be entering, not as findings about Casanare itself.

Discrimination also restricts livelihoods: reporting states that discrimination limits trans women mainly to hairdressing or sex work, and trans women in Caquetá have few options beyond sex work. Comparative context from the region places Colombia's statutory position ahead of most neighbours, while its homicide rates for trans people remain among the worst.
localsOnly:
Residents of Casanare exercise the same national rights as the rest of Colombia. Adults can change legal gender before a notary without surgery, with a free simultaneous name change on the first request, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025. Passports issued within Colombia offer male, female and X options since August 2023.

Same-sex marriage has been available since the Constitutional Court's ruling of 28 April 2016, with full adoption rights and dual-parent birth registration granted by a November 2015 ruling. Three rulings between February 2007 and April 2008 had already granted same-sex couples property, social-security and pension rights. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry ordered all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country.

Gays, lesbians and bisexuals have served openly in the armed forces since a 1999 court ruling. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a 2011 law bans discrimination based on sexual orientation. The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Casanare Department source yielded no usable finding on trans issues, so every claim in this record is national or drawn from other departments. No Casanare-specific data on violence, police conduct, or facilities was located, and whether the national protection machinery functions in the department is unresolved on the present sources.

National kill figures are not disaggregated by department in the inventory, so Casanare's share of the recorded homicides is not sourced. The Caquetá and Guajira armed-group campaigns are documented for those departments; their presence in Casanare is not established either way.

The inventory does not resolve how the November 2025 "trans" and "non-binary" identification markers are handled by notaries or the Registraduría in practice in the department, nor whether screening at entry points exposes a visitor's marker.
